description: We are Software Engineering students . Our interest in agriculture began with a university project, where we had the opportunity to explore the agricultural sector. This experience pushed us to dig deeper. When we discovered NASA's field shift challenge we saw an opportunity to strengthen our knowledge using real Earth observation data, and explore how technology can contribute to greener, more sustainable agricultural solutions in a world facing growing environmental and climate challenges.
summary:
Across Tunisia’s semi-arid farmland, many small farmers plant the same cereal season after season, out of habit, because inputs are cheap, or because nobody has shown them a better option. Over time this drains groundwater, depletes soil nitrogen, invites pests and leaves harvests exposed to the droughts and heatwaves that climate change is making more frequent.

Clover closes the gap between space data and the field. It starts from a single plot and asks what should come next, then answers with a short list of multi-year rotation plans built for that piece of land. To build them, it reads several years of NASA observations of rainfall, temperature, soil moisture and plant vigour over the plot, alongside soil characteristics and regional planting calendars. Each plan is tuned to what the farmer values most: saving water, protecting the soil or securing income.

The farmer sees which crop to sow and when, why one sequence beats another, what could go wrong, and roughly how much water, fertiliser and emissions they could avoid. For farmers who prefer talking to typing, a voice assistant understands spoken Tunisian Arabic and replies aloud.

Clover does not replace agronomists. It gives farmers and extension workers a shared, evidence-based starting point that makes satellite science usable at the scale of one family field, encouraging gradual shifts toward legumes and diversified rotations that rebuild soil fertility and make every drop of water count.
details: Clover is a web app that helps Tunisian farmers choose which crops to plant next, turning NASA Earth observation data into a crop-rotation plan they can understand and act on. A farmer draws their field on a satellite map (or uploads a soil-lab PDF, which is read automatically), selects the crops they can grow and sets their priorities, such as saving water, yield, soil health or climate resilience. The backend then gathers data for that exact location: daily climate from NASA POWER (rainfall, temperature and evapotranspiration), rainfall from GPM IMERG, soil moisture from SMAP L4 and vegetation health (NDVI) from MODIS, all accessed through Google Earth Engine. It combines these with ISRIC SoilGrids soil estimates and FAO crop calendars and parameters. A transparent rule engine then excludes unsuitable crops, generates multi-year rotations with sowing and harvest dates, and ranks three options. Each option comes with scores for water, climate, soil, erosion and crop-succession compatibility, plus pros, cons and risks. An impact calculator estimates the water, nitrogen fertiliser and CO₂e saved compared with continuous wheat. A voice assistant lets farmers ask questions aloud in Tunisian Derja, shows live English subtitles and can answer by voice. A key creative choice is that the AI only interprets the question and phrases the answer: every number comes from the deterministic engine, never from the language model. The intended impact is to help small farmers in a semi-arid, water-stressed country save water, depend less on synthetic fertiliser, keep their soils fertile and adapt to climate change, without needing technical training. We built it with React, Vite, Leaflet and Recharts on the frontend, Python with FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, MySQL 8 and JWT authentication on the backend, the Google Earth Engine Python API, Groq (language understanding and explanations), Gemini (document extraction), ElevenLabs (speech) and the browser's Web Speech API. It is a web app that needs no special hardware, just a browser and an internet connection. Our team designed for local language and literacy, poor connectivity (results are cached), transparency (every data source is shown and missing data is flagged rather than guessed), data privacy (all API keys stay on the server), and agronomic caution: parameters are labelled as indicative and are meant to be validated by agronomists.
